content: Azithromycin injection is a macrolide antibiotic approved by the FDA for treating community-acquired pneumonia and pelvic inflammatory disease. It is indicated for infections caused by susceptible strains of specific microorganisms. For community-acquired pneumonia, it is effective against pathogens such as Chlamydia pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella pneumophila, Moraxella catarrhalis, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae. For pelvic inflammatory disease, it targets Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Mycoplasma hominis. If anaerobic microorganisms are suspected, an additional antimicrobial agent with anaerobic activity should be used alongside azithromycin. The recommended adult dose for community-acquired pneumonia is 500 mg intravenously once daily for at least two days, followed by oral azithromycin at 500 mg daily to complete a 7-10 day course. For pelvic inflammatory disease, the dose is 500 mg intravenously daily for one or two days, followed by 250 mg orally daily to complete a 7-day course. The transition to oral therapy should be based on the physician's discretion and clinical response. Culture and susceptibility tests should be performed before treatment to identify the causative organism and its susceptibility to azithromycin. Therapy may begin before test results are available, but adjustments should be made once results are obtained. To prevent drug-resistant bacteria, azithromycin should only be used for proven or strongly suspected bacterial infections. Azithromycin injection is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to azithromycin, erythromycin, or any macrolide antibiotic. Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, angioedema, and severe dermatologic reactions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, have been reported. In rare cases, fatalities have occurred. Allergic symptoms may recur after discontinuation of symptomatic treatment, necessitating prolonged observation and management. Pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including azithromycin, and should be considered in patients presenting with diarrhea after antibiotic use. Common adverse reactions include gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Injection site reactions, including pain and local inflammation, are also common. Rarely, serious skin reactions, hepatotoxicity, and QT prolongation have been reported. Laboratory abnormalities, such as elevated liver enzymes and changes in blood counts, have been observed but are generally reversible upon discontinuation. Azithromycin interacts with certain drugs. Aluminumand magnesium-containing antacids reduce peak serum levels of orally administered azithromycin. Concurrent use with theophylline, digoxin, ergot derivatives, or drugs metabolized by the cytochrome P450 system may require careful monitoring due to potential increases in serum concentrations or pharmacologic effects. Co-administration with warfarin may enhance anticoagulant effects, necessitating monitoring of prothrombin time. In pregnancy, azithromycin is classified as Category B by the FDA. Animal studies have not shown harm to the fetus, but adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. There is no specific FDA guidance on its use during labor, delivery, or in nursing mothers. Pediatric and geriatric use has limited data, but pharmacokinetics in older adults are similar to younger adults. Sodium content in the injection may be clinically relevant for patients with conditions like congestive heart failure. Azithromycin acts by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible microorganisms, inhibiting protein synthesis without affecting nucleic acid synthesis. It concentrates in phagocytes and fibroblasts, potentially aiding drug distribution to inflamed tissues. Pharmacokinetic studies show that azithromycin achieves therapeutic concentrations in plasma and tissues, with a long tissue half-life contributing to its efficacy.
